publications.title: The Data Advantage: Enabling Australia's Research Impact. ARDC Year in Review 2026
publications.abstract: Discover how data is powering Australian research in our Year in Review 2026, The Data Advantage: Enabling Australia’s Research Impact. We share how we’re building national digital research infrastructure, advancing AI capabilities for researchers, and strengthening partnerships across research, government and industry. Explore how our Thematic Research Data Commons, national cloud services and skills programs are helping Australian researchers find solutions to real national challenges, from health and food security to biodiversity monitoring. Contents A Message From Our Chair A Message From Our CEO Delivering on the ARDC Strategy ARDC in Numbers ARDC Impact Case Studies and Success Stories People Research Data Commons Planet Research Data Commons HASS and Indigenous Research Data Commons Accelerating Research Translation ARDC Nectar Research Cloud National Information Infrastructure Digital Research Skills Published in November 2026. Year in Review 2026 covers July 2025 to June 2026. View the webpage and online case studies.

publications.title: Large Language Models in Museum Communication: Opportunities, Risks, and Implementation Requirements
publications.abstract: The transition of museum institutions into the era of generative artificial intelligence is characterized by systemic transformation, from the representation of digitized collections to dynamic interaction within a synthetic digital environment. Under these conditions, the challenge of adapting traditional standards of museum authenticity to the stochastic nature of large language models (LLMs) becomes particularly pressing. This study aims to develop a conceptual understanding of the transformation of museum communication, identify the epistemological challenges posed by the algorithmic generation of context and meaning, and describe mechanisms for preserving institutional authority as neural network–based tools are integrated into the public sphere. The study draws on a synthesis of institutional and communication approaches, which makes it possible to consider the museum not only as a custodian of material heritage but also as an active mediator amid increasing information noise. The empirical basis of the study consists of an analysis of the practical and educational agenda of the Hermitage School of Communication, held in Petrozavodsk in September 2025. The methodology involved identifying the professional competencies required to work in a hybrid media environment and evaluating practical applications of media analytics carried out by museum professionals using readily available AI tools designed for end users. The findings indicate that the adoption of LLMs inevitably shifts the focus of museum work away from routine content creation toward critical verification, strategic planning, and the management of meaning-making narratives. The stochastic nature of these models was found to give rise to risks of semantic uncertainty, including the loss of historical context, the reproduction of latent biases, and the substitution of factual information with probabilistic constructs. At the same time, the study illustrates the high effectiveness of algorithms in media analytics tasks, such as clustering audience inquiries and identifying latent patterns in unstructured feedback data. A key determinant of success is not only the model's technological capabilities but also the quality of research design established by the specialist when formulating the prompt. The findings point to the need to reconsider assumptions about the extent to which intellectual work in the cultural sector can be automated. An approach is proposed in which AI operates within bounded environments of verified museum data. The need for museums to adapt their infrastructure is also highlighted, including the creation of secure digital corpora, the implementation of transparent protocols for labeling synthetic content, and the development of ethical principles. The study emphasizes that, in the era of synthetic communication, the critical thinking and in-depth expertise of museum professionals remain particularly valuable resources.

publications.title: Rag n' Roll: A Framework to Evaluate Indirect Prompt Manipulation Attacks against RAG-based Applications
publications.abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique commonly used to equip LLMs with out-of-distribution knowledge by collecting, indexing, retrieving, and providing to the model specific information useful to answer user questions. The knowledge is often collected from public document repositories, providing a gateway for indirect prompt injections: attackers may craft documents specifically optimized to control the generated answer. In this paper, we investigate the practical performance of optimization techniques in hijacking the outputs of RAG pipelines. First, we review the frameworks commonly used to build RAG applications, derive a prototypical architecture, and identify critical parameters. We then examine prior work, seeking techniques for performing indirect prompt manipulations. We adopted five techniques across two macro-families and evaluated the criteria used to assess their effectiveness. With this knowledge, we implement Rag-n-Roll , a framework to evaluate the end-to-end results of LLM-based pipelines, introducing new metrics to better understand the benign or malicious nature of the generated answers. Our results show that established evaluation practices are insufficient to precisely assess attacks against RAG-based pipelines, leading to overestimates of their success. Furthermore, while attacks on the default configuration can successfully control up to 70% of the generated answers, we show that these performances depend heavily on previously ignored pipeline parameters. Finally, we distill our findings into actionable tips for developers looking to harden their RAG pipelines.

publications.title: DreamLander: A 6-DOF World Model based Reinforcement Learning Planetary Lander
publications.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.

publications.title: Ride-time inequalities for the event-based formulation of the dial-a-ride problem
publications.abstract: The paper investigates the model structure of the event-based mixed-integer programming formulation of the Dial-a-Ride Problem. We find that the design of events allows introducing new valid inequalities on the ride times. Time progression is modelled using Big M constraints which lead to a weak LP relaxation and deteriorate the solution process. The newly introduced valid inequalities deal with this issue and allow reducing the computation times by up to 99% for benchmark instances (a-X* instances) in comparison to the state-of-the-art event-based model formulation. To evaluate the potential of the new valid inequalities, we increase the time windows on the benchmark set by another 15 minutes and evaluate the model on the same instances with a time-related objective function where the Big-M-influenced time variables directly occur in the objective function. Even for the large time windows only two instances could not be solved to optimality within two hours (final gaps of at most 0.8%). With the time-oriented objective the largest average computation time with our valid inequalities was 74 seconds.

publications.title: Trajectory Density Ratios under Weak Support: A Survey across the Sciences
publications.abstract: Many problems across the sciences compare two stochastic processes through the sequences they generate. Reinforcement learning asks what a new policy would return from the trajectories of an old one; molecular simulation asks how much more a ligand binds from samples of the unbound state; climate attribution asks how a heat wave shifted under warming; and language-model post-training asks what a deployed agent will do from logged interactions. In every case, one quantity would answer all these questions at once: the ratio of the two probability laws over their generated sequences, the trajectory density ratio. This ratio exists only under strong conditions. When one process reaches states the other cannot, the ratio does not exist; when their overlap is thin, its variance grows without control with the sequence length; and when they concentrate on different lower-dimensional sets, the ratio is undefined altogether. Weak support of this kind is the norm for sequence data, not a sampling accident, and its price is paid in identifiability rather than in noise alone. This survey organizes the field around a three-level diagnosis of weak support and a map of the nine retreats that methods take when the full ratio is out of reach, from direct estimation and reweighting through staged decomposition, stationarization, and partial-identification bounds to smoothing, transport couplings, operator spectra, and direct estimation of a single functional. Each retreat keeps part of what the ratio offers and pays for the rest, and each application domain has standardized the retreat its data force. The survey closes with open problems: testable diagnostics at every level, partial identification at the trajectory level, a rate theory of time-amplified error, and benchmarks with ground truth.

publications.title: Prospective Action-Resource Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Electric HGV Fleets under Shared Charging Infrastructure
publications.abstract: Electric heavy goods vehicle (eHGV) fleet coordination requires each vehicle to choose driving, charging and resting actions whose consequences depend on shared infrastructure. Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) methods mainly represent current states, leaving action-specific futures and resource interactions to be learned indirectly. We develop Horizon-Preview and Graph-Coordinated Proximal Policy Optimisation (HGC-PPO), which integrates horizon preview and candidate-resource graph coordination into the PPO decision architecture. Horizon preview represents each legal action through its short-horizon operational consequences. Graph message passing then updates these candidates through station, charger-type and time-slot resources shared across the fleet. On the 794km Folkestone-Glasgow task, HGC-PPO achieved the lowest mean charging cost among five RL methods at £504.32 per vehicle, with a fleet completion time of 24.920h. It also completed the task 1.763h faster and cost £36.51 less per vehicle than a replay-verified finite-budget MILP benchmark. Across six unseen routes and fleet sizes from 5 to 20 vehicles, HGC-PPO delivered the lowest macro-average completion time, charging cost and charging frequency among the RL methods. A 2 by 2 ablation showed that the full preview-graph architecture performed best across all four operational metrics. These results show that prospective action information and fleet-wide resource coordination improve eHGV decisions under charging and driver-hours constraints.

publications.title: FAIR Institutional Repository Metrics (FIRM) - Conceptual Requirements
publications.abstract: The FAIR Institutional Repository Metrics (FIRM) project brings together UK universities to define what the FAIR Principles mean in practice for research datasets described by institutional repositories. Building on work by FAIRsharing and the Oxford University Research Archive (ORA), participating institutions reviewed and refined a common set of FAIR metrics against their different repository systems, metadata practices and requirements. This document presents the resulting FAIR Benchmark for Institutional Repository Datasets: a transparent, community-defined approach for assessing dataset metadata and identifying how its FAIRness can be improved. It distinguishes between FAIR features provided by repository infrastructures as standard and those dependent on information supplied for individual records, allowing assessment results to support practical guidance for both repository teams and researchers. The benchmark is designed to be reusable and adaptable. This first release focuses specifically on research datasets, providing a shared starting point for institutional repositories while allowing for different technical implementations and community priorities. Future work will explore extending the approach to additional digital research object types, building on the community-led process established through FIRM. The benchmark can support both automated FAIR evaluation and broader repository improvements.
